extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners reading examiner guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for USPTO examiners on preparing complete, clear, and procedurally correct Office actions, citing references, responding to applicant arguments, and indicating allowability of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and pinpointing of electronic documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations to electronic documents should include sufficient locating information such as claim numbers, figure numbers, chemical formula numbers, mathematical formula numbers, table heading numbers, gene sequence numbers, and computer program listing numbers if available; specific headings within the document structure (e.g., Best Mode of Performing the Invention or Industrial Applicability) can be indicated if page, paragraph, and line numbers are not available; specific passages can be indicated if the document format includes pagination or an equivalent internal referencing system, or by the first and last words of the passage cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office copies of an electronic document must be retained if the same document may not be available for retrieval in the future (important for Internet/online databases). If an electronic document is also available in paper form it need not be identified as electronic unless desirable. Examples (1-16) illustrate citation formats for various online/CD-ROM/Internet sources; include paragraph numbers (e.g., [0068]) or example numbers when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of office copies for electronic sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Office copies of an electronic document must be retained if the same document may not be available for retrieval in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially important for Internet and online database sources. Retain copies to ensure future retrieval and evidentiary support for citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective dates of declassified printed matter
rubrics_metrics.description: When using declassified material as references, consider both printing date and publication (release) date; the date of release following declassification is the effective date of publication within the meaning of the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The printing date may be prima facie evidence of prior knowledge for 35 U.S.C. 102(a) even if material was classified at that time, but printing date may be antedated by affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131. If release date not apparent, determine by reference to Office of Technical Services, Department of Commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorrect citation of references — correction procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an error in citation of a reference is brought to attention, a correcting letter with a correct copy of the reference is sent to applicant; if discovered by the examiner applicant is notified and the reply period is restarted; the examiner must correct the error in ink in the paper where it appears and initial the margin along with notation of the paper number of the corrected action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraphs 7.81–7.83 may be used to correct citations or supply copies. Every correction MUST be reflected on a corrected or new PTO-892. If an erroneous foreign patent citation, General Reference Branch may assist in determining correct country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation of decisions, orders, memorandums, and notices
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing court decisions use the USPQ citation and, when convenient, the U.S., CCPA or Federal Reporter citation; avoid citing manuscript decisions not available to the public; a federal district court decision reversed on appeal cannot be cited as authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If citing a manuscript decision available to the public but unpublished, give the rendering tribunal and complete identifying data (e.g., Ex parte — — , decision of the Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences, Patent No. — — — , paper No. — — , pages). Decisions found only in patented files should be cited only when no published decision exists on the same point. When citing Director’s orders or memoranda not incorporated into the manual, give title and date and other data as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of examiner’s action
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner’s action must be complete as to all matters, except in appropriate circumstances (misjoinder, fundamental defects, etc.) where action may be limited; matters of form need not be raised until a claim is found allowable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow 37 CFR 1.104. Limitations to full action are allowed in specified circumstances; ensure completeness except where justified by listed exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete action on formal matters in first Office action
rubrics_metrics.description: Any form that lists informalities and any additional formal requirements the examiner desires to make should be included in the first action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making formal requirements, the action should call attention to 37 CFR 1.111(b) and state that a complete reply must either comply with all formal requirements or specifically traverse each requirement not complied with. Use form paragraph ¶7.43.03 for allowable-subject-matter-but-form-requirements-outstanding situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language to be used in rejecting claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim is refused for any reason relating to the merits it should be 'rejected' and the ground of rejection fully and clearly stated, and the word 'reject' must be used. The examiner should designate the statutory basis for any ground of rejection by express reference to a section of 35 U.S.C. in the opening sentence of each ground of rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is rejected as broader than the enabling disclosure, give the reason; if rejected as indefinite, point out where indefiniteness resides; if incomplete, specify missing elements or what is required to render it complete. See MPEP §706.02(i),(j),(m) for specific language. Avoid omnibus or vague expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of personal remarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything of a personal nature must be avoided; examiners should not express opinions in the record that the application is devoid of patentable subject matter or express doubts about allowability of allowed claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if examiner considers disclosure lacking in merit, avoid expressing personal views in the record. As part of first Office action on the merits, identify any claims judged allowable and suggest amendments to make rejected claims allowable—failure to do so implies no allowable claim exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improperly expressed rejections to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: An omnibus rejection 'on the references and for the reasons of record' is stereotyped and usually not informative and should be avoided; do not group a plurality of claims together in a common rejection unless equally applicable to all claims in the group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific grounds for each rejection, tailored to the claims affected, to be informative to applicant and to the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note all outstanding requirements in every Office action
rubrics_metrics.description: When taking up an amended application for action the examiner should note in every letter all the requirements outstanding against the application; every prior point still applicable must be repeated or referred to prevent implied waiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include requirements for information under 37 CFR 1.105 and MPEP §704.10; determine whether any such requirement has been satisfied (e.g., by negative reply under 37 CFR 1.105(a)(3)). Upon finding allowable subject matter, correction of all informalities then present should be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer all material traversed
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner must provide clear explanations of all actions taken during prosecution. Where requirements are traversed or suspension requested, the examiner should reference them properly. Where applicant traverses any rejection and the examiner repeats it, the examiner should take note of applicant’s argument and answer the substance of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant’s arguments are persuasive and the rejection is withdrawn, the examiner must provide reasons in the next Office communication referring specifically to pages/lines of applicant’s remarks which form the basis for withdrawing the rejection. Do not merely indicate that 'all of applicant’s remarks' form the basis. Use appropriate form paragraphs (e.g., 7.38.01, 7.38.02). If withdrawing prior rejection results in allowance, include the reasons in a reasons for allowance (see MPEP §1302.14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Answering asserted advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: When applicant argues that prior art does not teach or inherently yield one or more advantages urged to warrant issuance, the examiner should state reasons if the asserted advantages are not sufficient to overcome the rejections of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State reasons in the record (preferably in the action following the argument) so applicant and the Board know the advantages were considered. Treat affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132 per MPEP §716 et seq. Use form paragraphs 7.37–7.38 series as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments Are Not Persuasive (¶7.37 general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant’s arguments filed have been fully considered but they are not persuasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must address all arguments not already responded to in the statement of rejection and provide explanation as to non-persuasiveness (fill bracketed text in form paragraph). This paragraph must precede many of the specific unpersuasive-argument form paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpersuasive Argument: Age of Reference(s) (¶7.37.01)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contentions that the references are old are not impressive absent a showing that the art tried and failed to solve the same problem notwithstanding its presumed knowledge of the references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use In re Wright precedent as guidance. Precede with ¶7.37.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpersuasive Argument: Bodily Incorporation (¶7.37.02)
rubrics_metrics.description: The test for obviousness is not whether features of a secondary reference may be bodily incorporated into the structure of the primary reference; nor that the claimed invention must be expressly suggested in any one or all references; rather, the test is what the combined teachings of the references would have suggested to those of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Briefly restate applicant’s arguments and then explain why bodily incorporation is not required. Precede with ¶7.37. See In re Keller.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpersuasive Argument: Hindsight Reasoning (¶7.37.03)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although any judgment on obviousness is in a sense necessarily a reconstruction based on hindsight, it must take into account only knowledge within the level of ordinary skill at the time the invention was made and must not include knowledge gleaned only from the applicant’s disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the examiner’s conclusion is not improper hindsight. Precede with ¶7.37. See In re McLaughlin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpersuasive Argument: No Teaching, Suggestion, or Motivation To Combine (¶7.37.04)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness may be established by combining or modifying teachings of the prior art where there is some teaching, suggestion, or motivation to do so found either in the references themselves or in the knowledge generally available to one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain where the teaching/suggestion/motivation is found (either in the references or in general knowledge). Cite In re Fine, In re Jones, and KSR. Precede with ¶7.37.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpersuasive Argument: Nonanalogous Art (¶7.37.05)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference must either be in the field of the applicant’s endeavor or, if not, be reasonably pertinent to the particular problem with which the applicant was concerned to be relied upon as a basis for rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the reference alleged to be nonanalogous and explain why it is analogous art. Precede with ¶7.37. See In re Oetiker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpersuasive Argument: Number of References (¶7.37.06)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliance on a large number of references in a rejection does not, without more, weigh against the obviousness of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the combination is proper; precede with ¶7.37. See In re Gorman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpersuasive Argument: Applicant Obtains Result Not Contemplated by Prior Art (¶7.37.07)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that applicant has recognized another advantage which would flow naturally from following the suggestion of the prior art cannot be the basis for patentability when the differences would otherwise be obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Briefly restate applicant’s arguments and explain why the result does not confer patentability. Precede with ¶7.37. See Ex parte Obiaya.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpersuasive Argument: Arguing Limitations Which Are Not Claimed (¶7.37.08)
rubrics_metrics.description: Features upon which applicant relies that are not recited in the rejected claim(s) cannot be used to patentably distinguish the claims from the references; limitations from the specification are not to be read into the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recite the non-claimed features and specifically point out how the language of the claims patentably distinguishes them from the references. Precede with ¶7.37. See In re Van Geuns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpersuasive Argument: Intended Use (¶7.37.09)
rubrics_metrics.description: A recitation of intended use must result in a structural difference between the claimed invention and the prior art in order to patentably distinguish the claimed invention; if prior art structure can perform the intended use, it meets the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Briefly restate applicant’s intended-use argument and explain why it does or does not patentably distinguish the claim. Precede with ¶7.37.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpersuasive Argument: Limitation(s) in Preamble (¶7.37.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: A preamble is generally not accorded patentable weight where it merely recites the purpose of a process or the intended use of a structure and where the body of the claim can stand alone without the preamble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restate preamble recitation in question and explain why it is not given patentable weight. Precede with ¶7.37. See In re Hirao and Kropa v. Robie.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpersuasive Argument: General Allegation of Patentability (¶7.37.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant’s general allegations that the claims define a patentable invention fail to comply with 37 CFR 1.111(b)/(c) because they do not clearly point out the patentable novelty in view of references or objections nor show how amendments avoid such references or objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate that general allegations are insufficient and point to regulatory requirements for specificity. Precede with ¶7.37.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpersuasive Argument: Arguing Against References Individually (¶7.37.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: One cannot show nonobviousness by attacking references individually where the rejections are based on combinations of references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why attacking individual references is insufficient when the rejection is based on combinations. Precede with ¶7.37. See In re Keller and In re Merck & Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Piecemeal examination should be avoided
rubrics_metrics.description: Piecemeal examination should be avoided as much as possible. The examiner ordinarily should reject each claim on all valid grounds available while avoiding undue multiplication of references; major technical rejections (lack of disclosure, lack of enablement, serious indefiniteness, res judicata) should be applied where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a major technical rejection is proper, state it with full development of reasons rather than a mere conclusion. Situations where limited action on claims may be appropriate include: (A) application too informal for complete merits action; (B) undue multiplicity of claims with no successful election request; (C) misjoinder of inventions with no successful election request; (D) perpetual motion disclosures—cite best prior art and explain pertinency. Where a sound prior-art rejection discloses the 'heart' of the invention, minor secondary rejections ordinarily should not be made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notify of inaccuracies in amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should notify applicants of inaccuracies in amendments as appropriate (see MPEP §714 II.G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to the cited MPEP subsection for procedures and example language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each claim to be mentioned in each Office action
rubrics_metrics.description: In every Office action, each pending claim should be mentioned by number, and its treatment or status given; each action should include a summary of the status of all claims presented for examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Form PTO-326 'Office Action Summary'. Claims retained under 37 CFR 1.142 and 1.146 have special treatment (see MPEP §821–821.04(b)). Keep the Index of Claims up to date (MPEP §719.04).

rubrics_metrics.name: State when claims are allowable; constructive assistance to pro se applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: When it becomes apparent that patentable subject matter exists in a pro se application, the examiner should draft one or more claims for the applicant and indicate such claims would be allowed if incorporated; in general, when claims disclose patentable subject matter but cannot be allowed due to defects in form, the examiner should not merely object or reject but offer definite suggestions for correction and may suggest interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this especially to inventor-filed applications to expedite prosecution. For 'allowable except as to form' situations, the examiner may note unclaimed aspects that if properly claimed may receive favorable consideration. If a claim is otherwise allowable but dependent on a canceled or rejected claim, state it would be allowable if rewritten in independent form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early allowance of claims (examiner-drafted claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner is satisfied after the search that patentable subject matter is disclosed and applicant intends to claim it, the examiner may draft claims considered to distinguish patentably over the art of record and present them to applicant for consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present drafted claims with explanation; this may encourage interviews and early agreement on allowable claims. Follow relevant form paragraph structure for presenting drafted claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of form paragraphs for corrections and replies
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific form paragraphs (e.g., 7.81–7.83, 7.82.01, 7.37–7.38.02, 7.37.01–7.37.13, 7.43.03) exist to standardize corrections, supply copies, and state the examiner’s position regarding applicant arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate form paragraphs per the situation: correcting citations, supplying copies of references, indicating arguments not persuasive, withdrawing previous rejections, or making new grounds of rejection. Ensure the applicable bracketed content is filled with specific references (pages/lines/claim numbers/statutory bases).
